answer: Overall: the plan is clear and honest but reads as a concept with untested assumptions. Improve it by replacing hedged language with evidence, numbers, and specific commitments. Priority improvements: (1) Quantify the market. Replace 'several hundred cities' and 'low thousands' with a bottom-up model: number of target cities by region, price per tier, realistic penetration, sales cycle length, and resulting ARR at years 1-3. Show the math and label assumptions. (2) Prove the core signal works. The entire value rests on utility-plus-mail data yielding accurate vacancy scores, yet no validation is reported. Add accuracy results from the prototype (e.g., precision/recall against a field-verified sample in one city), the method used, and known failure modes (seasonal occupants, vacation homes, mixed-use buildings, USPS flag lag). (3) Resolve data access, the biggest risk. Specify which utility providers have been contacted, their responses, any letters of intent, data format and frequency, cost, and the fallback if utilities refuse. Name the actual mail-status source and its licensing terms. State the legal/privacy position concretely (applicable state laws, utility data-sharing restrictions, aggregation approach) rather than 'we believe we are on safe ground.' (4) Convert interest into demand evidence. 'They said the idea was useful' is weak. Report number of interviews, specific pain points and budgets cited, any willingness-to-pay quotes, and secure at least one LOI or signed free pilot with defined success metrics before submitting. (5) Sharpen differentiation. Name specific competitors, compare features and price in a short table, and explain why a larger vendor or a university partnership could not replicate this quickly. Identify a defensible moat (proprietary data agreements, validated model, grant-application workflow, local relationships) rather than 'simplicity and price.' (6) Make the business model concrete. Define tiers, a draft price list by city size, unit economics (data cost per city, hosting, support time), gross margin, and how procurement works (thresholds below competitive-bid limits, grant-funded purchases, sole-source possibilities). (7) Present real financials. Add a simple 24-month budget, burn, use of funds tied to the ask (itemized: data, legal, hosting), break-even point, and milestones the prize would unlock. (8) Strengthen the team and go-to-market section. Explain how the team will get its first ten customers (conferences, state municipal leagues, planning associations, regional councils), name candidate advisors or approach plans for a government-sales mentor, and clarify founder commitment and time availability as students. (9) Tighten structure and tone. Lead with a one-sentence value proposition and a traction snapshot, cut qualifiers like 'rough,' 'modest,' and 'we believe,' and replace them with specifics or explicit 'to be tested by X date' statements. Add a risks-and-mitigations section (data access, privacy, slow municipal sales cycles, accuracy disputes) so reviewers see the risks are understood and managed. (10) Show the outcome for the customer. Include a sample map or output, a case example showing how a vacancy list supports a grant application, and a clear ROI argument (e.g., cost of the subscription versus staff hours saved or grant dollars won).
